fit_listing_widths(font_size_half_points = 16L) is the font size in half-points (8pt is 16L); the default is 18L (9pt); a smaller font fits more characters across the same sheet.
fit_listing_widths(size_half_points = ) is the superseded name of font_size_half_points: it still works, is not warned, and wins when both are given.
fit_listing_widths(total_width = 60) is the character budget for the whole listing, gutters included; NULL (the default) computes it from page, font and font_size_half_points.

fit_listing_widths(labels = c(USUBJID = "Unique Subject ID")) gives the words for source variables in data that carries no label attributes; a column's header is still derived from them, joined with its separator and wrapped to the width just fitted, and the width fit measures them.

fit_listing_widths(header_lines = 4) (default 4) is how many lines a header may reasonably occupy: a column is asked to be at least wide enough for its header at that height; a lower value buys more width, header_lines = Inf asks nothing for the header beyond its unbreakable token, and it never overrides a width the author set.
fit_listing_widths(min_width = 8) (default 6) is the narrowest a fitted column may be.

fit_listing_widths(probs = 1) (default 0.9) is the quantile of a column's cell widths taken as its demand: the default lets one unusually long value wrap instead of widening the column, and 1 takes the maximum.
fit_listing_widths(data = 1:3) (not a data.frame or tibble) stops: "`data` must be a data.frame or tibble; got 'integer'."
fit_listing_widths(spec = "spec") stops: "`spec` must be a listing_spec(); got 'character'."
fit_listing_widths(data = <a build_listing() body>) stops: "`data` has already been through build_listing(); fit the widths on the source data instead."

fit_listing_widths(labels = "no names") (not a named character vector, or with an empty or NA name) stops: "`labels` must be a named character vector mapping SOURCE column names to labels, e.g. c(USUBJID = "Unique Subject ID")."
fit_listing_widths(header_lines = 0) (not a single number of at least 1, or Inf) stops: "`header_lines` must be a single number >= 1, or Inf."
fit_listing_widths(min_width = 0) (not a single positive integer) stops: "`min_width` must be a single positive integer."
fit_listing_widths(probs = 2) (not a single number in [0, 1]) stops: "`probs` must be a single number in [0, 1]."
fit_listing_widths(total_width = -1) or a vector of two (not a single positive number) stops: "`total_width` must be a single positive number of characters."

fit_listing_widths() with a budget too small for the columns to be fitted stops: "A total width of <n> character(s) leaves <m> for the <k> column(s) to be fitted, which cannot each be <min_width> wide.  Widen the page, shrink the font, or set the widths yourself."
fit_listing_widths(page = 3) (not an rtf_page() or a list) stops: "`page` must be an rtf_page() object or a list of page settings."
fit_listing_widths() on a page whose margins leave no writable width stops: "The page's margins leave no writable width."
fit_listing_widths() with a font whose character width cannot be measured stops: "Could not measure the width of one character in font "<font>"."
collapse_repeats(x, cols) on an rtftable sets the repeated values in the chosen columns to NA, keeping the first row of each run, removes no row and leaves other columns untouched.

collapse_repeats(x, cols = c("grp", "sub")) is hierarchical: columns are processed in the order given (outermost first), the first on its own value, each later one on its combination with the earlier ones, so a change in any earlier column resets the run of every later one.
collapse_repeats(cols = ) takes character column names and/or integer positions in the table's final body columns; a list() mixes them (a bare c() would coerce the numbers to strings).

collapse_repeats() on a list of pages (an as_rtftables() result) collapses each page independently, so a run restarts at every page break, and gives what as_rtftables(x, collapse_repeats = cols) gives.
collapse_repeats() on an rtftable of several data frames (data_list) collapses each frame afresh, so the first row of each frame shows its value.

collapse_repeats(cols = "nope") (a column not in the table) stops: "`collapse_repeats` column 'nope' not found in the table."; an integer position out of range stops: "`collapse_repeats` index 9 out of range (1..2)."

collapse_repeats(x = <a data.frame or anything but an rtftable or list of pages>) stops: "`collapse_repeats()` expects an rtftable or a list of rtftable pages (as returned by as_rtftables() / as_rtftable()); build the table first."
catx(sep, ...) joins its arguments element by element with sep, so catx("/", "COMPLETED", "UPPER", "HYPERGLYCAEMIA") is "COMPLETED/UPPER/HYPERGLYCAEMIA"; sep is a single string, "" (none) allowed.
catx() leaves out every missing (NA) or empty ("") value, so the separator never appears doubled or at the start or end, and an element with nothing to join is "" (not "NA").
catx() strips leading and trailing blanks from each value before joining, as SAS CATX does (unlike ydisctools::catx()); a value of only blanks counts as empty.
catx() is vectorised over its arguments: a length-1 argument is recycled to the longest, and the result is a character vector as long as the longest argument.
catx() takes a factor by its labels, not its level codes, and any other input by as.character().
catx("/") with no values, or with only a zero-length vector, returns character(0).
catx("/", c("A", "B"), c("x", "y", "z")) (lengths that cannot be recycled) stops: "All arguments must be the same length, or length 1: got 2, 3."
catx() with sep missing, not a character, of length other than one or NA stops: "`sep` must be a single string."

listing_col(label = ) and its width change what the label means: a single string with no breaks is wrapped to the column's width, a character vector or a string carrying its own breaks is a layout left as written, and with no width a single string stays one line.

listing_col(layout = "flow") changes what width does to the cell and its derived header: with a width the separator is a break opportunity and short parts share a line, with no width both layouts return the text as it stands.
listing_col(width = 20) with fit_listing_widths(): a width the author set is kept and taken out of the budget first, and only the columns without one are fitted around it.
A column's header is taken in this order: listing_col(label = ), then fit_listing_widths(labels = ), then the variable's label attribute, then its name.

listing_col(sep = , align = , layout = ) win over listing_spec(sep = , align = , layout = ) for that column; a column that sets none (NULL) takes the listing's, and the listing's NULL takes the type's template.
listing_spec(type = "multiline") supplies defaults and any argument given explicitly (sep, spacer, spacer_rel_width, blank_row, blank_row_first, align, layout, wrap, record) overrides the template's.
listing_spec(wrap = f) replaces the type's own rule for the cells and for the derived headers alike; the rule is not mixed.
listing_col(rel_width = ) wins over width as the column's relative width in the rendered table; without it rel_width is width, then the longest line of label.

as_rtftables(listing = , col_rel_width = ) and the other arguments the caller passes win over the ones the listing derives (widths, header, alignment); an explicit split = "none" is left alone, so no pagination happens.
as_rtftables(collapse_repeats = ) given by the caller wins over the columns marked with listing_col(collapse_repeats = TRUE).
as_rtftables(blank_row_first = ) given by the caller wins over listing_spec(blank_row_first = ).
fit_listing_widths(total_width = ) wins over page, font and font_size_half_points, which are ignored when it is given; size_half_points wins over font_size_half_points.

as_rtftables(x, listing = spec) with an x that is already a build_listing() body is not resolved by order: it stops, "`data` was already built by build_listing(), and carries its own listing spec.  Drop the `listing` argument, or pass the unbuilt source data."
listing_spec(spacer = , spacer_rel_width = ) change what fit_listing_widths() has to spend: the gutters print, so they come out of the character budget before any column is fitted.

listing_col(collapse_repeats = TRUE) with blank rows: the value is carried into the record's blank row as well, so the run goes on between two records of the same value and the repeat is blanked; with listing_spec(blank_row = FALSE) the key still collapses across records.
listing_col(collapse_repeats = TRUE) on a key column to the right of another key column that wraps: the lines of one record are one value, so the carried key prints once per record.
Numbers as text: rounding (half away from zero or to even), significant digits, counts with percentages, parentheses aligned, NA as text.

round_num() rounds a numeric vector to digits decimal places by the package's one rounding rule, half to even as base R does or half away from zero as SAS does, and returns a numeric vector the same length as x.
round_num(x, rounding = "r") rounds an exact half to the even digit as base::round() does: c(0.5, 1.5, 2.5, -0.5) gives 0, 2, 2, 0 and -2.5 gives -2.
round_num(x, rounding = "sas") rounds an exact half away from zero as SAS ROUND() does: c(0.5, 1.5, 2.5, -0.5) gives 1, 2, 3, -1 and -2.5 gives -3.
round_num(x, rounding = "sas") absorbs the binary representation error of a decimal half the way SAS's fuzz does: round_num(2.675, 2, rounding = "sas") is 2.68 where "r" gives 2.67.
Away from an exact half the two rounding families give the same value: round_num(x, 2) with x = c(1.234, 5.6789, -3.14159, 100.001) is the same under "r" and "sas".
round_num(x = ) takes a numeric vector (double or integer) and keeps its length; NA stays NA and Inf stays Inf (round_num(c(NA, Inf), 1, rounding = "sas") is NA, Inf).
round_num(digits = ) is the number of decimal places and is 0 by default, so round_num(2.5) is 2 under "r" and 3 under "sas".
round_num(digits = ) larger than 0 rounds to that many decimals (round_num(2.675, 2, rounding = "sas") is 2.68).
round_num(rounding = "r") and round_num(rounding = "sas") are the two families; the case is not significant, so "SAS" is "sas" and "R" is "r".
round_num(rounding = NULL), the default, reads getOption("rtfreporter.rounding"), which is "r" unless the session or site set it; an explicit rounding wins over the option.

round_num(rounding = ) other than "r" or "sas" stops: "`rounding` must be \"r\" (half to even, as base::round() does) or \"sas\" (half away from zero, as SAS ROUND() does)."; the same stop comes from a bad option value when rounding is NULL.
round_num(digits = ) that is not a single non-negative integer (negative, NA, a vector, text) stops: "`round_num(digits = )` must be a single non-negative integer."
round_num(x = ) that is not numeric stops: "`round_num()` rounds numeric input; got character." (the class, or classes joined with "/").
round_num(digits = ) read as an integer: a fractional value such as 1.9 is cut to 1, with no message.
notes: the help says nothing of a fractional digits; as.integer() truncates it

statement: fmt_round() rounds numbers to digits decimal places and prints all of them, trailing zeros included, as a character vector the same length as x.
fmt_round() prints every requested decimal: fmt_round(c(2.5, 20.333, 100), 2) is "2.50", "20.33", "100.00".
fmt_round(digits = ) is the number of decimal places and is 2 by default.
fmt_round(digits = 0) prints no decimal point: fmt_round(2.5, 0) is "2" under "r" and "3" under "sas".
fmt_round(rounding = "r") rounds an exact half to even: 23.445 is "23.44", 2.675 is "2.67", 0.125 is "0.12".
fmt_round(rounding = "sas") rounds an exact half away from zero: 23.445 is "23.45", 2.675 is "2.68", 0.125 is "0.13", -2.675 is "-2.68".
fmt_round(rounding = NULL), the default, follows options(rtfreporter.rounding) (23.445 at 2 digits is "23.45" under "sas", "23.44" under "r"); the option's case is not significant.
Away from exact halves fmt_round() gives the same text under "r" and "sas".
fmt_round(na = "") is the text for NA and NaN, an empty string by default; a given text replaces both.
fmt_round() prints Inf and -Inf as "Inf" and "-Inf".
In a vector with NA, fmt_round() gives the na text at the NA's place and formats the other elements as usual.
Negative numbers keep their sign: fmt_round(-2.675, 2, "sas") is "-2.68".
fmt_round() never writes scientific notation and does not depend on options(scipen) or options(digits): fmt_round(1e5, 1) is "100000.0".
fmt_round(x = ) that is not numeric stops: "`fmt_round()` formats numeric input; got character. Character columns are taken as already formatted -- leave them alone."
fmt_round(digits = ) that is not a single non-negative integer stops: "`fmt_round(digits = )` must be a single non-negative integer."
fmt_round(rounding = ) other than "r" or "sas" stops with the message of round_num() (FR-FM110).
fmt_signif() renders numbers to digits total printed digits, the integer part included, as a character vector the same length as x.
fmt_signif() counts the integer part in the digits: fmt_signif(c(0, 10.2, 103.4, 20.333333, 23.4463), digits = 4) is "0.000", "10.20", "103.4", "20.33", "23.45".
fmt_signif() keeps trailing zeros: 10.2 at 4 is "10.20", 5 is "5.000", 500 is "500.0".
An integer part longer than digits prints whole: fmt_signif(12345.6, 4) is "12346" and 987654.3 is "987654" (decimals are never below zero, integer digits never dropped).
When rounding carries a value into another decade the decimals are recomputed: 99.995 at 4 is "100.0" and 9.9999 is "10.00".
With small = "signif" a value below 1 that rounds up to 1 is recomputed too: 0.99996 at 4 is "1.000".
Negative numbers count the digits of their magnitude: -20.333 at 4 is "-20.33" and -0.5 is "-0.5000".
Zero prints digits - 1 decimals under both values of small: fmt_signif(0, 4) is "0.000" and fmt_signif(0, 1) is "0".
fmt_signif(digits = ) is the total of printed digits and is 3 by default.
fmt_signif(small = "signif"), the default, counts a value below 1 from its first significant digit: 0.333333 is "0.3333", 0.0004567 is "0.0004567", 0.00998 is "0.009980" at 4 digits.
fmt_signif(small = "fixed") applies the integer-counting rule to values below 1: 0.333333 is "0.333", 0.0004567 is "0.000", 0.00998 is "0.010" at 4 digits.
fmt_signif(rounding = "r") rounds an exact half to even and fmt_signif(rounding = "sas") away from zero: 23.445 at 4 is "23.44" and "23.45".
fmt_signif(rounding = NULL), the default, follows options(rtfreporter.rounding).
fmt_signif(na = "") is the text for NA and NaN, an empty string by default: na = "NE" gives "NE" for both.
fmt_signif() prints Inf and -Inf as "Inf" and "-Inf".
fmt_signif() never writes scientific notation and does not depend on options(scipen) or options(digits): fmt_signif(123456, 6) is "123456" and 1e-4 at 4 is "0.0001000".
A plan's significant-digit token (for instance {mean:.3s}) prints the same text as fmt_signif() for every value, under both rounding families.
fmt_signif(x = ) that is not numeric stops: "`fmt_signif()` formats numeric input; got character. Character columns are taken as already formatted -- leave them alone."
fmt_signif(digits = ) that is not a single non-negative integer stops: "`fmt_signif(digits = )` must be a single non-negative integer."
fmt_signif(small = ) other than "signif" or "fixed" stops with match.arg()'s error.
fmt_numeric() turns the selected numeric columns of a data frame into text with fmt_signif() or fmt_round(), one rule for all cells or one per row key, leaving every other column as it was.
fmt_numeric(data, cols, signif = 4) replaces the selected numeric columns by character columns formatted as fmt_signif() does: c(24, 902.3312, 230.1234) is "24.00", "902.3", "230.1".
fmt_numeric() keeps the row count, the column order and every column outside cols.
The text fmt_numeric() makes renders as written, without scientific notation, and is the text set_decimal_split() splits on.
fmt_numeric(cols = ) names the columns to format, by name or by position.
A column in cols that is not numeric is left alone, and when none of them is numeric the data is returned unchanged.
fmt_numeric(signif = ) without by formats every selected cell to that many total digits, as fmt_signif().
fmt_numeric(digits = ) without by formats every selected cell to that many decimals, as fmt_round(): digits = 1 gives "24.0", "902.3", "230.1".

fmt_numeric(by = ) names a single carrier column, by name or position, whose values key into formats; it may be the row-heading column itself, matched after trimming ("  Mean" keys on "Mean"), and it is left untouched.
fmt_numeric(formats = ) is a named list of rules, each a list with exactly one of signif or digits and optionally small.
fmt_numeric(formats = list(.default = )) covers every key that has no entry of its own.
A rule in formats may carry small, which overrides the call's small for that rule: list(signif = 4, small = "fixed") on 0.0004567 gives "0.000".
With by, a row whose selected cells are all missing needs no key, so a group-label or blank row is not an error and gets the na text.
fmt_numeric(small = ) is "signif" by default or "fixed", the same as in fmt_signif(), for the signif form and for rules that do not name their own.
fmt_numeric(rounding = ) is "r", "sas" or NULL (the option rtfreporter.rounding), applied to every cell: 23.445 at digits = 2 is "23.45" under "sas".
fmt_numeric(na = "") is the text for a missing numeric cell, an empty string by default.
An Inf or -Inf in a selected cell prints as "Inf" or "-Inf".
fmt_numeric(data = ) that is not a data frame stops: "`fmt_numeric()` needs a data frame."
Without by, fmt_numeric() with neither or both of signif and digits stops: "Give exactly one of `signif` or `digits` (or use `by` + `formats`)."
fmt_numeric(by = , signif = ) or (by = , digits = ) stops: "Give either `by` + `formats`, or `signif` / `digits` -- not both."
fmt_numeric(by = ) without a non-empty named formats list stops: "`fmt_numeric(by = )` needs a named `formats` list."
fmt_numeric(by = ) naming more than one column stops: "`fmt_numeric(by = )` must name a single column."
A formats entry that is not a list stops: "`fmt_numeric(formats = )` entry 'n' must be a list, e.g. list(signif = 4)."
A formats entry without exactly one of signif and digits (none, or both) stops: "`fmt_numeric(formats = )` entry 'n' must give exactly one of `signif` or `digits`."

A non-missing cell whose key matches no formats entry, with no .default, stops naming the keys: "`fmt_numeric()`: no format for 'x'. Add it to `formats`, or a `.default` entry." ("them" for several keys).

fmt_numeric(cols = ) or (by = ) naming a column that is not there stops: "`fmt_numeric(cols)` column 'zz' not found in the table." (by: `fmt_numeric(by)`); a position out of range stops: "`fmt_numeric(cols)` index 9 out of range (1..3)."
fmt_numeric(signif = ) or (digits = ) or a rule's signif / digits that is not a single non-negative integer stops: "`fmt_numeric(signif = )` must be a single non-negative integer." (digits likewise).
fmt_numeric(rounding = ) other than "r" or "sas" stops with the message of round_num() (FR-FM110).
fmt_count_pct() formats count and percent pairs as "n (xx.x)" strings of one display width, the closing parenthesis in the same column, padded with non-breaking spaces.
A percent from 0 to below 10 prints with one integer digit: fmt_count_pct(5L, 5, pct_unit = "percent", nbsp = " ") is "  5  (5.0)".
A percent from 10 to below 100 prints with two integer digits: fmt_count_pct(14L, 50, pct_unit = "percent", nbsp = " ") is " 14 (50.0)".
A percent of 100 or more prints as a whole number: fmt_count_pct(30L, 100, pct_unit = "percent", nbsp = " ") is " 30  (100)".
A count of 0, or a missing or infinite percent, prints the count alone with no parenthesis, padded to the cell width: fmt_count_pct(5L, NA_real_, na = "-", nbsp = " ") is "  5       ".
Every cell is 10 characters wide with the closing parenthesis at column 10, whichever branch it takes.
fmt_count_pct(count = ) is a numeric vector of counts; a length-1 count is recycled against pct.
fmt_count_pct(pct = ) is a numeric vector of percents, a fraction in [0, 1] by default; a length-1 pct is recycled against count.
fmt_count_pct(pct_unit = "fraction"), the default, multiplies pct by 100 (0.5 prints "50.0").
fmt_count_pct(pct_unit = "percent") takes pct as already 0 to 100.
fmt_count_pct(pct_sign = TRUE) puts a "%" before the closing parenthesis and makes every branch one character wider (11), so the parenthesis still aligns; FALSE is the default.
fmt_count_pct(nbsp = ) replaces the padding spaces; the default is the non-breaking space U+00A0, and " " keeps plain spaces.

fmt_count_pct(na = "") is the text printed when the count is missing (NA or NaN): "" gives an empty cell, "-" gives "  -       ", the token right-justified in the count field and padded to the cell width (11 with pct_sign).

fmt_count_pct(rounding = ) rounds the percent once to one decimal with "r" or "sas" before the branch is chosen: 1/16 (6.25 percent) prints "6.2" under "r" and "6.3" under "sas"; NULL follows options(rtfreporter.rounding).
A real count with a missing percent still prints, on its own; a missing percent is not missing data.
An Inf or -Inf count prints as "Inf" or "-Inf" in the count field and is not replaced by the na text.
The width branch follows the rounded percent: 9.96 percent prints as 10.0 in the two-digit branch, and 99.96 prints as "100" in the whole-number branch.
Zero-length count and pct give a zero-length character vector.
fmt_count_pct(count = , pct = ) not both numeric stops: "`count` and `pct` must both be numeric."
fmt_count_pct(count = , pct = ) of different lengths, neither of length 1, stops: "`count` and `pct` must have the same length (or one of them be length 1)."

fmt_count_pct(pct_unit = "fraction") with a finite pct above 1 warns once per session: "`fmt_count_pct()`: `pct` has values above 1 but `pct_unit` is \"fraction\" (0..1), so 5 prints as 500.  Pass `pct_unit = \"percent\"` for values in 0..100."; NA and Inf do not trigger it.

fmt_count_pct(na = ) that is not a single non-NA string stops: "`na` must be a single string -- the text printed for a missing value (e.g. \"-\" or \"NA\").  \"\" (the default) leaves the cell empty."
fmt_count_pct(pct_unit = ) other than "fraction" or "percent" stops with match.arg()'s error; fmt_count_pct(rounding = ) other than "r" or "sas" stops with the message of round_num() (FR-FM110).
format_count_pct() is the deprecated old name of fmt_count_pct(), kept until 0.9.0, with the same arguments and the same output.
format_count_pct() returns what fmt_count_pct() returns for the same arguments.
The first call in a session warns: "`format_count_pct()` is deprecated: it is `fmt_count_pct()` now, with the same arguments.\n  Removed in 0.9.0."; later calls are silent.
format_count_pct() passes pct_unit, nbsp, pct_sign, na and rounding on to fmt_count_pct().
realign_count_pct() is deprecated until 0.9.0 (as_rtftables(align_count_pct = TRUE), the cell format "count_pct", does the same): it re-pads "n (xx.x)" strings to the widths of fmt_count_pct().
realign_count_pct() reformats every cell of the form "n (xx.x)" through fmt_count_pct(pct_unit = "percent"), so all matching cells share one width.
A cell of the form "n (xx.x%)" keeps its "%" and the whole column is aligned with it, the closing parenthesis last.
The cell forms follow fmt_count_pct(): "12 (100.0)" becomes the whole-number branch and "0 (0.0)" the count alone; surrounding whitespace in the cell is ignored.
A cell that does not match the pattern, such as "not a count", "NE" or "NA (NA)", is returned unchanged and unpadded.
NULL and a zero-length x are returned as they are, and a non-character x is converted with as.character().
realign_count_pct(nbsp = ) is the padding character, the non-breaking space by default, as in fmt_count_pct().
realign_count_pct(na = "") leaves a missing cell as it is (NA stays NA).
realign_count_pct(na = "-") right-justifies the token in the count field for a missing cell and for a cell that already holds the token: "  -       ".
The token follows the column's percent sign: with any "n (xx.x%)" cell in the column the token cell is 11 characters wide.
In a column with no count and percent cell the token is returned as it is, with no padding.
The first call in a session warns that realign_count_pct() is deprecated and points to as_rtftables(align_count_pct = TRUE) (the message ends "Removed in 0.9.0."); later calls are silent.
realign_count_pct(na = ) that is not a single non-NA string stops with the message of FR-FM195.
fmt_count_paren() aligns cells of an integer count followed by a parenthetical: the counts right-justified, the text inside the parentheses right-justified, every other cell unchanged.

fmt_count_paren(c("1 (1.2%)", "0", "11 (3.6%)", "108 (35.3%)")) right-justifies the counts to 3 and the inner text to 5 (cells "  1 ( 1.2%)", " 11 ( 3.6%)", "108 (35.3%)") and leaves the lone "0" as it is.
The parenthetical may be any notation; mixed "( 2.8%)", "(100%)" and "(<1%)" in one column align to equal width.
A cell that is not an integer count with a parenthetical (a lone count, "75.2 (8.6)", "Mean (SD)", "n/a", an empty cell) is returned byte for byte unchanged, without non-breaking spaces.
An empty x is returned as it is, and a non-character x is converted with as.character().
fmt_count_paren(bare = FALSE), the default, leaves a cell with no parentheses as it is.
fmt_count_paren(bare = TRUE) also pads a bare integer count into the count field, to the cell width, so it lines up under the parenthetical cells: "  0        ".
fmt_count_paren(nbsp = ) replaces the padding spaces in the cells it reformats; the default is the non-breaking space and " " keeps plain spaces.
fmt_count_paren(na = "") turns a missing cell into an empty string.

fmt_count_paren(na = "-") prints the token right-justified in the count field, its right edge under the ones digit, padded to the column's cell width, whether bare is TRUE or FALSE; a two-character token ends on the ones digit too.
A token wider than every count widens the count field, and the cells keep one width: na = "N/A" gives "N/A       " beside "  1 (1.2%)".
A cell that already holds the na token is aligned like a missing cell; other text, "NE" or "n/a", stays unchanged and unpadded.

fmt_count_paren(na = ) that is not a single non-NA string stops: "`na` must be a single string -- the text printed for a missing value (e.g. \"-\" or \"NA\").  \"\" (the default) leaves the cell empty."
fmt_count_paren_bare() is the deprecated spelling of fmt_count_paren(x, bare = TRUE), kept until 0.9.0, with the same output.
fmt_count_paren_bare() also pads a bare lone count into the count field: c("1 (1.2%)", "0", "11 (3.6%)", "108 (35.3%)") all have one width.
fmt_count_paren_bare(x, nbsp, na) is byte for byte fmt_count_paren(x, nbsp, na, bare = TRUE).
fmt_count_paren_bare(na = "-") aligns the token like fmt_count_paren(): c("1 (1.2%)", "0", NA) gives "1 (1.2%)", "0       ", "-       " (non-breaking spaces shown as spaces).
The first call in a session warns: "`fmt_count_paren_bare(x)` is deprecated: it is `fmt_count_paren(x, bare = TRUE)`, the same output.\n  Removed in 0.9.0."; later calls are silent.
fmt_value_paren() aligns cells of any text value followed by an optional parenthetical, the padding before the "(" so every ")" lands in one column.
The value before the parenthesis is right-justified, so its rightmost character lines up: c("86", "12 (14.0)", "1 (<1)", "n=3 (3.5)") gives " 86       ", " 12 (14.0)", "  1   (<1)", "n=3  (3.5)".
The whole "(...)" block is right-justified to a common right edge, the padding falling before the "(" and never inside; every ")" is in one column and decimal cells line up on the point.
A zero count drops its parenthetical: "0 (0.0)" prints as "0"; only an all-zero parenthetical is dropped, so "0 (BLQ)" keeps it.
A parenthetical that is a plain number of 100 or more loses its decimals: "(100.0)" is "(100)", "(100.0%)" is "(100%)", "(105.0)" is "(105)"; "(100)" stays.
A non-numeric parenthetical ("<100.0", "BLQ", "n/a") is not rewritten, only right-justified.
A cell with no parenthesis is right-justified in the value field and padded to the width of the parenthetical cells; a column of bare values is simply right-justified.

Cells fmt_value_paren() cannot parse are returned unchanged: an empty cell, a whitespace-only cell, a cell whose parenthesis is not last ("Mean (SD) by visit") and a cell with nothing before the parenthesis ("(100%)").
Nested parentheses are not parsed and the cell is returned unchanged; an empty x is returned as it is.
The 100 rule gives the text fmt_count_pct()'s whole-number branch gives (and realign_count_pct()): "12 (100.0)" and "6 (50.0)" align to the same text.
fmt_value_paren(nbsp = ) replaces the padding (and every other) space in the reformatted cells; the default is the non-breaking space and " " keeps plain spaces.

fmt_value_paren(na = "") turns a missing cell into an empty string; a token is a value like any other and is right-justified with the values: c("1 (1.2%)", NA, "108 (35.3%)") with na = "-" gives "  -        " in the second cell.
fmt_value_paren(na = ) that is not a single non-NA string stops with the message of FR-FM223.
fmt_right_align() right-justifies the non-empty cells of a character column to the width of the widest, padding on the left.
fmt_right_align(c("5", "120", "7", "")) gives "  5", "120", "  7", "": the cells are padded on the left to the widest.
An empty cell or a whitespace-only cell is left as it is and does not set the width.
An empty x, and a column of only empty or blank cells, is returned unchanged; a single value has nothing to align against and is unchanged.
A non-character x is converted with as.character(); in the padded cells every space, inside the text too, is replaced by nbsp.
notes: spaces inside a cell's text become nbsp as well, which the help does not say

statement: fmt_right_align(nbsp = ) is the padding character, the non-breaking space by default; " " gives plain spaces.
fmt_right_align(na = "") turns NA into an empty cell, as before.
fmt_right_align(na = "-") is right-justified with the other cells: c("5", "120", NA) gives "  5", "120", "  -".

fmt_right_align(na = ) that is not a single non-NA string stops: "`na` must be a single string -- the text printed for a missing value (e.g. \"-\" or \"NA\").  \"\" (the default) leaves the cell empty."

An explicit rounding = on a call wins over options(rtfreporter.rounding), in either direction: with the option "sas" a call with rounding = "r" rounds half to even, with the option "r" fmt_count_pct(rounding = "sas") prints 1/16 as 6.3.
In fmt_numeric(by = , formats = ), a rule's own small wins over the call's small for that rule.
With by, fmt_numeric() takes formats and refuses signif / digits; without by, signif or digits (exactly one) are the rule. Without by, a given formats is not read at all.
notes: formats is silently ignored when by is NULL

statement: small changes what digits means for a value below 1: "signif" counts from the first significant digit, "fixed" counts the integer part (as 0), so 0.0004567 at 4 digits is "0.0004567" or "0.000".
rounding changes which width branch a percent takes, because the percent is rounded before the branch is read: 9.96 percent takes the two-digit branch and 99.96 the whole-number branch.
pct_unit changes what pct means (0 to 1 or 0 to 100) and pct_sign widens every branch by one, so the closing parenthesis stays in the same column.
na and nbsp together: the padding of the na token cell uses nbsp like the other cells, so the token's right edge is under the ones digit in both settings.
na changes what bare means for a missing cell: a missing cell is aligned like a bare count whether bare is TRUE or FALSE, and a token wider than the counts widens the count field.
The na token follows the other cells of the column: it takes the column's percent sign and, when no cell of the column matches "n (xx.x)", is left unpadded.
